metadata.title: UV Space
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: Move, scale and mirror the address a shader looks up
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.

beats.narration_text: U V Space. Learn to move, scale, tile and mirror the address a shader looks up, so you can scroll a picture, zoom into it, and keep a circle round on any shape.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. Many people read U V as where a pixel sits on the screen. It is where the pixel sits on its shape. And since it is only a pair of numbers, you can change it before you use it. Everything else follows from that.

props.text:
UV says where a pixel is on
the screen.

beats.motion_claim: The writer types the assumption a newcomer arrives with and corrects it into the film's real subject.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. A pixel is one dot of the picture. A texture is an image a shader can read by address. A vector is a bundle of two to four numbers. And a uniform is a value your game sets from outside the shader.

terms.meaning: a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn
one dot of the picture on screen
an image a shader can read by address
a bundle of two to four numbers
a value your game sets from outside; every pixel sees the same one

qc.sparse_reason: TERMS card: prerequisites, one plain line each.

beats.narration_text: One picture, and it never changes. Yet here it slides, shrinks and repeats. The picture file is untouched. The shader only changed where it looks. That is the trick behind scrolling, zooming and tiling.

beats.narration_text: Every pixel on a shape has an address: two numbers, called U V. The first says how far across, the second how far down, each from zero to one. The top left is zero, zero. The bottom right is one, one.

shot.visual_intent: A square with U labelled along the top (a drawn arrow pointing right) and V labelled down the left side (a drawn arrow pointing down), corner labels (0, 0) at the top left and (1, 1) at the bottom right, and a terracotta dot whose live (u, v) label updates as it moves. Caption (GLOSSARY wording): 'UV: a point's address on the shape: 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down'.

shot.motion_claim: The dot slides across (U grows), then down (V grows), then jumps to the top-left corner and to the bottom-right corner, its label updating each time.

beats.narration_text: Notice that the second number counts down, the opposite of a school graph. And size does not matter: a tiny shape and a huge one both run zero to one. An address is a fraction of the shape, not a count of pixels.

A grey up arrow marked 'school graph' beside the small square and a terracotta down arrow marked 'V' beside the large one. Caption: 'fraction, not pixels'.

beats.narration_text: Here is every address at once, drawn as a color. Red is the first number, so it grows to the right. Green is the second, so it grows downward. Blue is held at half. Each pixel paints its own address.

beats.narration_text: To color a pixel, the shader can read a picture at that pixel's address. The texture function takes a picture and an address, and hands back the color stored there. That color becomes the pixel's.

An arrow runs from the ringed pixel to the same relative spot on the picture, where a terracotta dot lands; a teal swatch travels back along the arrow and the ringed pixel fills with teal. Small tag on the arrow: 'texture()'.

beats.narration_text: Inside fragment, which Godot runs once for every pixel the shape covers, we read the picture at that pixel's own address. Nothing is changed, so the picture comes out exactly as it went in.

Readout 'shader on' at the switch; then a terracotta ring settles on the sprite's square with the readout 'unchanged'.

beats.narration_text: Here is a way to hold it in your head. The picture stays put. The shape is a window onto it, and the address says where the window sits. Change the address, and the window slides.

beats.narration_text: In fragment, the address is read-only. So the pattern never changes: copy it into a variable, bend the copy, and look up the picture with the bent copy. Every trick from here fills in the middle line.

shot.visual_intent: A cream code card with the real seven-line template; focus lands on the function, then the copy line, then the empty bend line, then the lookup line as each is named.

beats.narration_text: Predict first. We subtract a quarter from the horizontal address. Which way does the picture go? Watch. It slides right, even though we subtracted. That feels backwards, so let's check the numbers.

A terracotta ring marks the sprite's fixed square.

beats.narration_text: Here is why. The pixel in the middle now looks up the spot a quarter of the way across. So whatever lives at that spot shows up in the middle. Everything lands a quarter further right.

beats.narration_text: So the rule is a reversal. Subtract from the horizontal address, and the picture moves right. Add to it, and it moves left. Change the address one way, and the picture goes the other.

First a terracotta arrow pointing right labelled 'subtract from U' with the dot moving right on the lower ruler; then an arrow pointing left labelled 'add to U' with the dot moving left. Persistent small tag: 'the opposite way'.

beats.narration_text: The same goes for the vertical address, with one twist. It counts downward, so subtracting from it sends the picture down. Subtract from both, and the picture moves right and down together.

beats.narration_text: What lies beyond one? By default, the lookup keeps returning the picture's edge pixels. Declare the texture with repeat enable, and the picture starts over instead. Scale by three, and you get a three by three grid.

beats.narration_text: A node's own texture has the same switch. It is called texture repeat. Set it to enabled, in the node's settings or in code, and that texture repeats too. Mirror is another setting: every other copy is flipped.

beats.narration_text: Now let it move on its own. Add a tenth of the time to the horizontal address. Time is seconds on one clock the whole game shares. The picture scrolls left, a tenth of its width every second.

beats.narration_text: Four moves, then. Subtract, and the picture moves one way. Add, and it moves the other. Multiply by more than one, and it shrinks. Multiply by less than one, and it grows. Always the opposite of what the address does.

beats.narration_text: Scaling keeps zero fixed, so zero is the pivot. Here zero is the top left corner, so everything grows away from that corner. To grow from the middle, the middle has to be zero.

beats.narration_text: In these coordinates, the length of the address is its distance from the middle. Closer than the radius means inside a circle. So a circle is one comparison, and the radius is the only number.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. U V is a pixel's address on its shape, from zero to one. Change the address one way, and the picture goes the other. Scale around zero, so put zero in the middle. Absolute value folds one side onto the other. Multiply by the aspect ratio, and a circle stays round. Repeat or a mask keeps the edges clean.
